utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Martinovic and Naletilic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The witness who is called to testify today requests some protective measures; first of all, pseudonym, and facial distortion. The witness lives in Mostar and has concerns as for his security and the security of his family. That's why I ask you to grant his request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I guess there is no objections from Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your request is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The registrar has a document with some details about our witness's background and a little bit more, because he was involved in some activities which should not be revealed here straightforwardly. So you will see a little bit more details on this sheet of paper.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The pseudonym for this witness is "U".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, your request for protective measures has been granted by the Trial Chamber. Now you are given a pseudonym. From now on during the trial, of course, you will be called "Witness U." By no means should you pronounce your full name or your first name during the trial. And now you will be shown a sheet of paper with some name and the indication of some activities that you were involved in during the war and after the war. Will you read it, but not read it aloud, and check if it is correct. If it is correct, you may say "yes."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honour, Witness U's testimony is supposed to go mostly to background, paragraph 7, 10 and 11; superior authority, paragraph 17; general allegations, paragraph 18 to 20; count 1, paragraphs from 26 to 28, 30, 31, 34(a), (b); counts 2 to 5 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down for the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Sorry. So count 1, paragraphs 26 to 28, 30, 31, 34(a), (b); counts 2 and 5, paragraphs 35 to 38, 40, 44; counts 15 to 17, paragraphs 51, 52.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, what is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: I'm a Bosniak by nationality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Who were your parents by religion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: My parents died before 30, and 15 years ago. And by religion, they were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness U, did you have any military background before the war broke out in the former Yugoslavia in 1991? I mean military background in the army of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: No, absolutely not, except that I, just like all young men of a certain age, served my regular military term in the former Yugoslav national army, the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: For how many years?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Fifteen months.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you live in Mostar through 1991-1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, I was born in Mostar, and I have spent my whole life right up to now in Mostar. And this includes the period that you are asking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness U, I would like to ask you, as a Mostar citizen, if you could give us a very brief overview of the main events that you personally observed, had knowledge of, for the fall of 1991 through 1993 in Mostar, first of all, which led to serious deterioration in the relations between the Croat and Muslim communities and, finally, brought about a conflict between the HVO and AbiH.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Of course I can. But there wasn't only a deterioration in the relationships between the Muslims and the Croats but between all three nationalities that lived in Mostar. Serbs also lived there. So there was a deterioration in relations between all the people which resulted in a bloody, difficult war. And if you would like, I can talk about this chronologically; or if you prefer, I could answer your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness U, don't hurry, please. Otherwise, the interpreter will stop you. I would like you just to narrate a little bit, but pay more attention to the relationship between the Muslim and Croat communities because it's mostly the subject matter of our case. I mean, main events.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Of course. I will try to slow down in order to enable the interpreters to keep up. It's very difficult to determine -- it's very difficult precisely to determine when the relationship amongst the groups deteriorated to such an extent that it turned into armed conflicts. In the fall of 1991, Mostar was occupied by forces of the former Yugoslav National Army, strengthened by a large number of so-called reservists, i.e., reserve soldiers, mostly from the Republic of Serbia and the Republic of Montenegro. Already, at that time, the citizens had a sense that something unusual or out of the ordinary was happening, and soon there was a major presence of these soldiers who did not look like real soldiers. This escalated through individual incidents. And then in the course of March and particularly April 1992, an armed conflict broke out between the citizens who, in part, spontaneously and, in part, in an organised fashion tried to oppose this evident threat. In May, the armed conflicts escalated and turned into a real war against the former Yugoslav National Army, or whatever was left of it. And the patriotically-oriented citizens of Bosniak and Croat ethnicity, and partially also citizens of Serb nationality who were citizens of Mostar, after a couple of months, these armed clashes went or turned in favour of the citizens of Mostar. And the armed formations, which had already started to form, or had already grown, so that at the end of June, Mostar, the main part of the city or the centre of the city, was liberated, liberated from those military or paramilitary forces. The summer of '92 came. The shelling of Mostar continued by Serb units who had taken the elevations surrounding the city. And in the very city itself, at the end of the summer and in the fall, there were small, minor incidents in the beginning between Croats and Bosniaks, mostly due to the fact that the Croats, who had never formed the majority in the city of Mostar. Never in the history of Mostar did they form the majority, and that's how it was before the war, so they wished to have absolute power. They wanted their military formations called "HVO" to be the dominant power in the military sense. The political leadership of the Croats --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honours, I must object at this time. I don't think there's a question in front of the witness. The witness seems to be rambling. The witness also seems to be giving conclusions or opinions. I believe this witness is a lay witness, not an expert witness, and I don't believe -- and I object to this witness giving conclusions and making conclusionary statements without any foundation. It's highly improper. The Prosecutor must ask specific questions and gain specific answers and not just let this witness talk. And I object to this form of testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, at the very beginning of the direct examination, it is quite necessary to lay out the foundations of the situation so that we could come into the particular environment at that time. Maybe the witness has talked a lot on those things, but we could ask him to be more concise in his answering of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I appreciate that, and I believe that is exactly my objection. I was silent while the background information was coming out, but at this point in time it's become more than background information. Now he's getting specifically into the areas concerned in our indictment and he is giving conclusions without any foundational basis at this time, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, will you please guide your witness with the specific questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, I will do it, but --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: But I do not agree with my learned colleague because, first of all, in the beginning of my direct examination, I informed the Trial Chamber that some of his testimony will be relevant to the background which is contained in our indictment. And as far as I remember, he is our first witness, a citizen of Mostar, here in the courtroom who can give some information about the background and the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. development of events. As for his conclusions, it's up to him to make his conclusions or not to make. The decision will be made by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you may proceed with the concise questions, and give more guidance to your witness in your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, I would like you just to return to the events in April 1992, when there were some conflicts in the military sphere of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: The conflicts in April 1992 were conflicts with the Serbian side. I am noting again that at that time there were no conflicts between Croats and Muslims or Bosniaks. I'm sorry if the Defence misunderstood me. I just tried, in five or six sentences, to present the period in a chronological manner from 1992 until May 1993, which you must admit is a large period to be encompassed by five or six sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: We'll stop on some certain events. First of all, the problem of the Territorial Defence of HOS and HVO forces, what was the reason for such conflict or discrepancies between these two factions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: HOS are the armed forces of the Croatian Party of Right, organised in the Republic of Croatia. The HVO appeared as the armed forces officially on the 8th of April, 1992. In order not to make any conclusions, I will demonstrate this in an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: So go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: At the end of March, the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina was formed as a regular armed force. And already in the month of April, the independent Mostar Battalion was also formed in Mostar as one of the units within the regular army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So I stopped at the point where I was talking about the company where I worked, which is of exceptional importance everywhere in the world. Already at the end of March, the company was occupied by members of the units which wore insignia as defence of the city. Over 90 per cent of that unit was composed of citizens of Croatian nationality from Mostar and the surrounding area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Were there any -- sorry. Were there any Muslims within this formation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: I didn't meet a single one, and I worked for almost 30 days in that company. I worked there, I slept there, because very few of us came to work. And in that time, I never saw a single Bosniak Muslim there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And what happened in your place of work? I mean what kind of implications did it have for you personally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Towards the end of April or, let's say, in mid-April, the director of my company at that time, who was a Bosniak Muslim and with whom I worked for about 20 years, told me that nobody asked him anything any more, that his duties were completely taken over by one lawyer, a citizen of Croatian nationality, and that because of the efforts of me, my efforts, and the efforts of my boss, both of us having worked for over a month to keep this large system together, this person could pay us ten monthly salaries as a kind of reward. And that was the only thing that this person could do for us, because probably most of us will be fired from our jobs, which came about in just a few days. The Bosniaks employed in that system were mostly fired, and other employees appeared, Croats, who up until that time did not work at that company in Mostar. I knew them from having seen them around before, because they usually -- most of them worked in the company's branches in Western Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And what about the situation with the distribution of humanitarian aid in Mostar area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Humanitarian aid in Mostar, since the very beginning, was at all times -- until the end of the war -- was quite inadequate to satisfy the most elementary requirements. In that regard, the people who were exposed to the most difficulties were Muslims and Serbs because the citizens of Croat nationality had the possibility to receive most of their humanitarian aid from charity organisations of the Catholic church, of course, with the assistance of many countries from Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: What about the freedom of movement in Mostar, in this area -- I mean this period, in 1993, in the beginning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: The only possible way out from Mostar for people aged between 18 and 60 was, of course, with the permission of the HVO, and these were particular, specific persons, especially the president of the defence section of Herceg-Bosna, the commander of the zone of South-Eastern Herzegovina, and the president of the Croatian Defence Council of the city of Mostar. By the end of 1992, the HVO adopted some decisions about the use to be made of abandoned apartments, and in early 1993, regulations regarding freedom of movement so that, in fact, the citizens of Bosniak ethnicity were not allowed to go out of the city or enter the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And what about abandoned flats? Which abandoned flats do you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: When I say "abandoned flats," Your Honour, it's very difficult to explain the situation. Mostar was full of refugees. There were Croats that had fled, but they were basically expelled Bosniaks from Eastern Herzegovina under the occupation of the Serb paramilitary forces. The decree, in fact, stipulated that further settlement was prohibited. In other words, absolute protectionism had been introduced because at that particular moment, the flats where the citizens of Mostar used to live and citizens that had left Mostar, because of the war situation, these people -- these flats were systematically given to citizens of Croat nationality who had mainly arrived from Central Bosnia and Northern Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you see all these documents, I mean the documents on freedom of movement and regulation of abandoned flats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: The city of Mostar, before the war, had only one paper -- newspaper that appeared once in a fortnight, once in 15 days. Of course, during the war, there were no papers appearing, no newspapers, and the only newspapers that could be bought were the papers coming from the Republic of Croatia. Those regulations were mainly published over the Croatian radio, the radio station in Mostar. Whether they were made available in a written form to some of the institutions, I cannot confirm truly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Who was the president of the HVO in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: The president of the HVO from the day the HVO was made public officially was Mr. Jadran Topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Will you spell it for the record.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: J-A-D-R-A-N T-O-P-I-C.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness U, do you know the facts when some Mostar citizens who were Muslim religion -- Bosniaks by nationality joined the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Of course, a large number of the citizens of Mostar of Bosniak nationality joined the HVO, particularly in the early period, because the HVO basically proclaimed the goals of the struggle, at least on paper in a declaratory fashion, goals that were agreeable with most of the citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you have relatives or your former colleagues, et cetera, who joined the HVO? I won't ask you to give any names, just the fact only, if you have someone.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Of course. A large number of my friends and acquaintances, and my younger brother, were members of the HVO until the first conflicts erupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: When did the first conflict erupt?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Not counting individual occasional incidents, the first conflict took place during the night between April 18th and 19th in 1993. Of course, I am referring to Mostar because as early as in 1992, there were conflicts, bloody conflicts north of Mostar. But in Mostar, the conflict began in the following manner: The HVO suddenly shelled and used infantry weapons to attack a small unit of the B and H army, which was located in the very centre of the city at the Mostar Hotel. The attack lasted until the morning hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And what was the result of that attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: The result of that attack was a compromise agreement supervised by UNPROFOR. And that unit left its base at the Mostar Hotel, which had to remain neutral. But two days later, it was taken over by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And where did the corps of the BH army have its headquarters, then, after that event?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: The command of the 4th Corps of the B and H army was in practically the same building as the command of the HVO in the western part of Mostar until there was an outright attack on Mostar. And when the small unit had left, the command of the 4th Corps of the army of B and H remained totally isolated and fully surrounded, which eventually ended in the capture of all the members of the unit and the seizure of all equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness U, it is established that the conflict, military conflict, which broke out in April 1993 was already in full swing in April, by the end of April. And what was happening in Mostar at that period of time? I mean the end of April 1993 and the beginning of May 1993.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: This was, so to speak, the time before the conflicts, and alongside with the evolution of the situation in Mostar, agreements and consultations were taking place, mainly in Geneva, because a multitude of plans were under review with the aim of putting a stop to the escalation of fighting in Bosnia and Herzegovina. On the basis of one of those plans, which provided for the organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina into Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. ten provinces - this was in early April 1993, I believe - the then Minister of Defence, Mr. Bozo Rajic, publicly stated on television a proclamation in the form of an order, according to which all the units of the -- the regular units of the B and H army had to fully abandon -- leave the area of Mostar or to place themselves fully under the command of the HVO of Herceg-Bosna. I mention that that agreement had never been signed by all three sides in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: But was this agreement or decision or order of the former minister ever implemented?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Of course it was not implemented, because it was illegal, it was illegitimate, and it was impossible to be implemented under those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And what happened in Mostar on the 9th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: On May 9th, 1993, in the morning hours, about 4.00 a.m., all the available forces of the Croatian Defence Council, the HVO, with possible support of some of the regular units of the Croatian army, attacked the command of the corps of the B and H army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: What kind of weapons was used by the HVO during that attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: All sorts of weapons, with the exception of the aviation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: To which place did you observe the attack? I don't ask you to give the name of your street.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: No, I will not, of course. I observed the attack from my building in the centre of the city, from the ninth floor. I had an excellent view and I could fully see the locations from which the HVO was acting and the left bank of the city that was in fire and smoke because it had been the target. The portion of the city on the left banks of the Neretva River, it was attacked by all sorts of conventional weaponry with which the HVO disposed, basically artillery weapons. The whole area was shelled systematically, which of course meant a number of civilian casualties and total destruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: How long did that attack last?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: The attack virtually didn't end at all. It was exceptionally fierce from 4.00 in the morning until noon, when the portion of the city on the left banks of the river, according to the assessments of that time and later on, about between five and seven thousand shells were in fact shot at -- fired at the city, with continuous infantry attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Were there any official statements made by the HVO authorities regarding the events that were happening on the 9th of May in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: The citizens were probably - and here I mean the citizens of Croat nationality, because I think that many of them had been surprised by that attack, and not only surprised but in fact appalled, at least I think this was the case with my neighbours - they were expecting an official explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours, I object to the non-responsiveness of this question. The question was very simply put: "Was there any official statement made by HVO authorities concerning the events of the 9th of May?" And there's no answer to that question. It's a non-responsive answer, and I object. I've been trying not to object, but I would ask the Trial Chamber to please ask this witness to listen to the questions and try to answer those questions and be responsive. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Witness, please answer the question. The question is a very simple one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, at 9.00 on the Croatian -- the radio station of Mostar, a proclamation was made, signed by the president of the HVO of Mostar, Mr. Jadran Topic. Well, just to give you the gist of it, the proclamation stated that the HVO had undertaken a widespread action with the aim of establishing law and order, and calling upon the Bosniaks, the Muslims, to put out white flags through their windows as a sign of capitulation, of surrender, of surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did anyone do that? I mean did anyone put white flags on their buildings, apartments, roads?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: I cannot give you an accurate response to that. But as far as I could see, and as far as I learned later on, no one had done it because this had no sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what sense there would have been for the citizens in the part of the city which was being fiercely shelled and who asked for any sort of shelter to survive would risk their lives to climb to their windows and put out white cloth as a sign of surrender, not knowing even who had attacked them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: But was there any other announcement by the HVO authorities of events on the day -- the first one you are talking about was in the morning. But the situation kept on developing for the worse, as I understood from your testimony.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes. The first proclamation which was announced, it was probably a mistake. It was never repeated again. In the evening hours, at prime time, that is when the news -- news were being broadcast, the television of Croatia, a programme which was, in fact, forced upon most of the citizens of that area, the public explanation was broadcast for this, not mentioning the early morning announcement. It said that the B and H army in the morning hours tried to attack a military building which served as a base of the HVO, and that the HVO responded fiercely and hit at the military target.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And what happened in Mostar between these two announcements, one in the morning and the second one later? What happened to the Muslim population, first of all, civilian population?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: At the very beginning of the attack - in some parts of the city, even before the attack - units of the HVO, which were very numerous, they were all available units that were not engaged in combat, they began to surround buildings, houses, and started to take out from those buildings all citizens of Bosniak nationality, including myself, regardless of our age. There was also a large number of mothers with children. They took them to the stadium of the Velez football club. It was like a central collection point from where they took them to already-prepared camps in buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: What happened to you on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Before 6.00 in the morning, the building where I live, and the entrance to my apartment actually leads to 51 apartments, so one HVO unit in full combat equipment came into this entrance. This means that they were wearing helmets, bulletproof vests. They were very well armed. My apartment was entered by about ten members of the HVO. They told me and my brother to lean against the wall. They kicked and pushed aside all the things that were in the apartment. They ransacked it, allegedly looking for weapons. While they were doing this, they took for themselves objects which could be of use to them, valuable objects, gold jewellery --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: For example.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: -- gold jewellery, a small Commodore, child's computer, and some other things which I didn't see them take because they were very rough. They were pulling drawers out. And then after 10 minutes, they told us to go out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did they explain to you why you and some other people should go out or must go out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: No. There was no explanation. They were just looking for weapons, and they told us that we have to go outside in front of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you see any people, both military or civilians, you were familiar with before down in the street where you were taken by the HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: They didn't take us down the street. They brought us outside in front of the entrance to the building where there was a large closed vehicle waiting, and the vehicle was marked as an urgent medical assistance vehicle. Of course, I recognised some of the HVO members who came into my apartment on May 9th, that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Could you recall their names now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Two of them were Bosniaks; one was called Dzemo Skobalj. I didn't know him personally, but I knew him from Croatian television because he was a member of the Croatian army already in 1992 and had taken part in the fighting around Dubrovnik. The second was called Galic [phoen] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, the screen did not pick up the name the witness just indicated. Two of these individuals were Bosniaks. One was called, and the transcript does not give the name of that person. Could we get that spelled for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor. You could clear it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Could you spell the name of the person you just named now, who was a Muslim and you knew him before.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: The first person I knew is -- it's D-Z-E-M-O S-K-O-B-A-L-J.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And the second one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: I didn't know the second person's name, but I knew that his last name was Orucevic, O-R-U-C-E-V-I-C.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you know the position he occupied at that time in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: I think they were members of the special units of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. Were you taken to Velez stadium as well, along with other civilians and Muslims, on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Of course. This covered vehicle, which could really fit only ten Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. people in it, received 35 of us, and that included myself and my brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And what happened, then, by the end of the day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: The vehicle went straight to the Velez stadium, entered this facility and came right up to the grassy area. There were hundreds of people on this grassy area, women, children, who had been brought in earlier perhaps from some other parts of the city. We were just told briefly to get out and to join those people. My brother and I were in such a position in that vehicle that we could only come out amongst the very last. Since we were the first ones to go inside the vehicle, so then we were amongst the last to come out. When it was my turn - I was already at the door of the vehicle - I heard the driver talking with my brother, and they called me to come back into the vehicle. The driver was wearing full military equipment. He had a helmet. His face was painted with some kind of paint so that neither I nor my brother recognised him. But he had obviously recognised my brother - perhaps he was with him in the same unit - because he called him by name. And he said that we shouldn't leave the vehicle, that he would take us back to the command of my brother's unit, and that if we did leave the vehicle, it was a question whether we would ever come out alive. And this is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: So you had the possibility of getting home on that day?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... go home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes. My brother reported to the commander and his deputy in an attempt to find out why he was taken away, and he just told us, "Go straight home. Don't go out anywhere, don't look out of your windows. Sit and wait. Something bad is happening." That was all. And then we ended up at our apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to the people who were kept at the Velez stadium on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Those people, amongst whom were a lot of my relatives because I have a very large family and my family has been living in Mostar for 400 years, they mostly ended up at the Heliodrom camp, the HVO camp at Heliodrom. Some went to other camps. Nobody was returned home from the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: How long were they kept in the Heliodrom camp? I mean, for example, your relatives who were arrested.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: They were kept there between five and fifteen days.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And what other events were happening in Mostar after the 9th of May? I mean now, first of all, the confrontation line. When did it appear in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: The confrontation line was practically established with the attack of the HVO, because except for the command of the 4th Corps, which remained completely encircled in the western part of Mostar and where all the soldiers and the officers were captured, the other units of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina remained on the other side of the street. The name of the street is "Bulevar," and it divides the town of Mostar in two because it goes down the middle of it. This is where the HVO established its observation posts, its bunkers and other military fortifications, practically.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And what about the civilian authorities at that time in Mostar; did they function after the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Sir, it's very difficult to talk about civilian authorities in war, knowing that the HVO practically -- is practically a military police, civilian, and all other types of authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you live far away from the confrontation line? I don't ask you to give your street, but the area, approximately.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: As the crow flies, it's perhaps about 150 to 180 metres from the line of separation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Could you point it out on the map if I show it to you, just without indicating again the street? Just point out the area you were living in.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Of course I could show you quite precisely the area and also the line which at that time was the line of separation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I would ask the usher to help me. It's Exhibit Number 11.18. Is it possible to place it on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, just be careful there. Do not point out the locations of his home.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Just the area, you may circle it and mark it with the number "1".

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: This area here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Just next to --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: So it's this area here that I'm pointing out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: So for the record, this area is close by Centur II. Yes? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's what that settlement was called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: It would be easier, I think, just to go into closed session so that this witness could specifically tell us where he lived, for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, that's a good idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Maybe we'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And what was happening on the confrontation line? What was its purpose?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: The purpose of all that was to attempt to capture the whole of the city of Mostar by the HVO, so on the line of conflict, the regular units of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina were -- practically stopped the further advance of the HVO. And you could say that as things developed, and right until the end of the war, there were many, many attempts to break through this line and to capture the whole of the town, which was absolutely the objective of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Were there firing and shooting on the confrontation line, sniping? Did you observe it while you were in Mostar in the area where you lived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Of course there was a lot of shooting. From the building where my sister lives, and which is about a hundred metres away from my building, from the seventh floor of an abandoned Bosniak apartment, a sniper unit was operating 24 hours a day practically, in shifts. These were people who were certainly not from Mostar. By their accent, it was easy to tell because they would greet each other as they were passing by my sister's apartment, who happens to be married to a Croat. They were operating right above her apartment. A couple of times, I saw them, but it was difficult, as you can imagine, to see other snipers. You could only see the effects of their activity because they operated from well-concealed positions. Shelling was on a daily basis. Part of the line was shelled that was controlled by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Even when there were negotiations about establishing some kind of a cease-fire, which practically never gave any results until March 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you observe any destruction in Mostar as a result of the shelling on the confrontation line or along the line of defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Sir, I didn't say that only the line of separation was shelled. The left bank of the river was shelled night and day from heavy artillery, heavy weapons. In order for you to have a picture of what that part of the -- that side -- what that bank looked like, we're talking about maybe some four or five kilometres in length and about 300 to 500 metres wide. That's the dimension of the area. So that part of the city was showered by hundreds of shells each day, so that about 90 per cent of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. accommodation facilities were destroyed. All key institutions were either completely destroyed or they -- or were burnt. There was no water, there was no electricity. There was no possibility of extinguishing the buildings that had been set on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, this set of questions is over. I would like to proceed with another one, but I see that the time of the break is coming up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, it is. We'll resume at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness U, do you know which HVO units were running the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Well, at the confrontation line, the -- practically all the HVO units alternated: the special-purpose units, the units of the military police and the other HVO units. That was basically the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Were there any specific areas of responsibility along the confrontation line and some units that were in charge of those areas; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes. In the very centre of the city, we can freely say in the most dangerous part of the confrontation line on the Croatian side, one of the -- an area of responsibility -- a part of the area of responsibility, perhaps 400 or 500 metres, were under the control of two special units of the HVO. "The anti-terrorist groups," they were called. One of them was the Benko Penavic group, and the other one was called "Vinko Skrobo" and its commander was Mr. Vinko Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: How did you get this knowledge about the division of the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Well, I gained that knowledge at the camp of -- the HVO camp at the Heliodrom, because many of my colleagues and members of my family went to the line of the HVO mainly in the part of separation in the city itself, and this is where I got my initial knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you. We will return to this subject a bit later. So you indicated two units, Vinko Skrobo and Benko Penavic. Who was in command of the Benko Penavic unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Mr. Mario -- Mario Milicevic, nicknamed "Bajo."

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: If you can spell this name for the record.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: For both commanders or just for one?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: For one.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: For the one you know, I suppose. So the commander of Vinko Skrobo was V-I-N-K-O, M-A-R-T-I-N-O-V-I-C. Of the Benko Penavic unit, the commander was M-A-R-I-O, M-I-L-I-C-E-V-I-C. Both had nicknames which were more commonly used, and people referred to them basically by their nicknames.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Could you specify the concrete area of responsibility of each of these two commanders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Martinovic's unit was located in the very centre of the city, basically in the area of the Medical Centre. This was a building, a polyclinic, and perhaps in the length of about 180 or 200 metres. South of it, in the unit of Gospin Park and in the direction of the Catholic church, there was the Benko Penavic unit. In the Santic Street, which continues towards the north, different units would alternate. This was an area belonging to the 2nd Battalion of the 2nd HVO Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know where Vinko Martinovic's base was located at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: As far as I know, it's main base was located in Kalemova Street in a cafe. I think it was called Mali Raj, and it was near a large

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I see that my monitor does not pick up the restaurant this witness just identified, and I wonder if, for the record, that could be cleared up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Is it very important to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Because I understand that there is some difficulties in picking up all those names by the interpreters and by the typists. All those names will be checked out at night. But since you said it's very important for your knowledge, then we may ask Mr. Prosecutor to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, could you repeat the name of the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Of course I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: The cafe where the base of the Vinko Skrobo unit was located was called Mali Ari in Kalemova Street, and this cafe was probably about 10 or 15 metres from the old and large restaurant called Ladovina, Stepan Zubac was the owner, and I believe that Mr. Martinovic's soldiers would be served meals there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And I would like to clarify the name of the street, because we have here Kali Street.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: No, the street's name is Kalemova. It is probably -- it is a combination of "Kale" and "street," and the name of the street is precisely Kalemova. K, it starts with a K.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you know which building was occupied by Vinko Martinovic himself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: The -- Vinko Martinovic occupied the Cafe Mali Raj. I think the former owner was called Cisic. This is a cafe at the entrance of the street 70 to 80 metres on the right-hand side. Kalemova Street is a side street which links up two very busy streets, and Kalemova Street is about 300, 350 metres long.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And what about Benko Penavic's base, where was it located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: The base of the unit Benko Penavic was at the Central Square, at the roundabout in Mostar called Rondo. It is a roundabout with six streets, two in a triangle, and that is where many Serb -- old Serb houses were located. And in one of those houses, the first of those houses actually, was the base of Benko Penavic. And it was owned by an old Serb family from Mostar called Pesko. I think that those houses had been nationalised following World War II.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the house which belonged before the war to the Kajtaz family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Pesko?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: No, I am talking about Kajtaz family. A different building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: The family house of the Kajtaz was in Kalemova street, very near the restaurant which housed the Benko Penavic unit. I don't know how this house was confiscated. And now it houses the Consulate of the Republic of Croatia. And Mr. Kajtaz, as far as I know, has been placed in an old people's home in the eastern part of the city, and is trying to get back his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Now, returning to the situation in Mostar among the civilian population, did HVO authorities allow Muslim civilians to leave the western part of Mostar for the eastern part of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: During the conflict, that is following May 9th, seven days later more or less, there were discussions between the military commands of the B and H army and the HVO. The negotiations were very intensive, and it appeared that the situation might calm down. In a short span of time of two or three days, the citizens were able to move from one bank to the other bank by bus. After that, and during the war, they could never do that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... was there a special prohibition of that account or it might be explained by some other reasons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Well, war operations were going on, on a permanent basis, and it appeared that the negotiations were not evolving as had been expected. The war operations intensified, and there were no longer any contacts between the citizens of one side and the other side, with the exception of possible visits by the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness U, were you ever arrested, I mean really arrested, during the war, apart from the first, let's say, arrest what happened on the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Of course I was. On June 30th, 1993, I was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And do you associate this day with some other event or only with your arrest?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: On that day, practically all men aged between 18 and 60 were arrested, but afterwards we learned that even younger and older men had been arrested - very few had in fact avoided arrest - and been taken away to prisons. I was personally taken to the camp in Heliodrom, where I remained until December 17th, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: What happened in Mostar that such kind of action started precisely on the 30th of June?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Well, sincerely speaking, this was an expected action of the HVO, because between May 9th and June 30th - I presume this was the end of May, beginning of June - on the local Croatian radio a proclamation was announced, signed by the new commander of the defence of Mostar, Zlatan Mijo Jelic. And from that proclamation, it was stated from that day onwards all apartments gravitating towards the line of separation would be proclaimed a war zone and would be put under the direct command and control of the HVO. In other words, the soldiers of the HVO could enter Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. any apartment, evict the tenants, and use these apartments for their own needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did AbiH undertake any military actions against the HVO after the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes. On May 30th, early in the morning, the units of the B and H army attacked and took over very important buildings of the HVO, the Sjeverni Logor Barracks and the region of Bijelo Polje, and in that way established a physical link towards Sarajevo, because until then the city had been totally surrounded, encircled.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness U, are you sure that it happened in May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: I think it was the end of May or beginning of June, in around that time. Well, you're talking about the occupation of the barracks. June 30th, in the morning hours, the barracks I was referring to and Bijelo Polje, this was the day I had been arrested and the day when many of the Bosniaks living in Mostar had been arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you remember the circumstances of your arrest of the 30th of June?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, very well indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Please, could you recount what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Of course. Because fighting had intensified that day - I already said that the building in which I lived was not far from the separation line - many bullets found their way there. And at about 11.00, I looked through the balcony, which is on the opposite direct where bullets could not penetrate, and I saw that the entrance of my building -- through the entrance of my building, soldiers were coming in, armed soldiers, with helmets, bulletproof jackets, and I knew what that meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you know to which units those soldiers belonged?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: There were two soldiers that came to my apartment. One of them I knew personally. His name was "Kemo Selmanovic," and he belonged to the KB, the Convicts' Battalion. I didn't know the other soldier, but from his accent in conversations with him, I could conclude that he was a young man from Western Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I would like you just to spell the name of the soldier who was familiar to you and --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Of course. His name was K-E-M-O, S-E-L-M-A-N-O-V-I-C.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you. How do you know that he was a member of the special unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Even before the conflict, I was a very good friend of his brother. His brother would tell me that his younger brother, as he expressed himself, was Tuta's soldier. And there were no problems in 1992 to know which soldier came from which unit, because the soldiers that belonged to special units like to boast about it. They had, of course, some advantages and privileges.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: For example, which kind of privileges and advantages that you know they had?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Well, I can give you some examples. There is one where one soldier belonging to the Vinko Martinovic, Stela, unit as early as 1992, in a cafe, for no reason at all shot dead a Bosniak, Dragan Bojcic, and was in no way held account -- brought to account for this. Had it been a member -- an ordinary member of the HVO, he would have been punished in some way or another. Against this person, no charges were brought, not even any disciplinary measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Where were you taken after the arrest?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: At the entrance of the building, they already asked for my personal documents. When they established that I was a Bosniak, a Muslim, they told me to go out in front of the building, to be questioned with their boss. When I went down, got in front of the building, I saw about 150 -- up to 200 people who were brought to that building. They were rounded up, and I couldn't see any boss there, nor did anyone speak to me on that occasion, nor did I have occasion to address anyone. We were simply told that we should wait there until further notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Were all the people gathered in that area Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you see among them any people that were familiar to you before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Absolutely. First of all, my neighbours. I said earlier that at the entrance to my building -- that the entrance to my building leads to 51 apartments. So practically all those people just from my entrance were taken out, and also an approximate number from other entrances. I knew the majority of those people. They were my closest neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: So you were told to wait until further notice. And what was that further notice, if any?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: No, we were just told to wait. It was already 1.00. The date was the 30th of June. The temperature was about 36 to 37 degrees in the shade. We were all standing in the sun. It was very hot.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Then where were you taken later in the afternoon or in the evening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: After about one hour more, so sometime at about 2.30, five buses arrived, and we were told to enter the buses, not to pay attention to the number of seats. A bus has an average number of 50 seats. There were about 70 to 80 of us in each bus. And this first column of five buses, where I was, also set out in the direction of the Heliodrom camp. Precisely speaking, it went to the place called Krusevo. This is where we left the buses and went on foot to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Could you explain what "Heliodrom" means to you? For what purposes was that complex used before the war, for what purposes is it used now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: The Heliodrom is an enormous space where the former Yugoslav People's Army had its units. It had its helicopter squadrons stationed there, which were quite numerous, as well as the accompanying units, anti-aircraft defence, and some others which protected those facilities. Because in the immediate vicinity is also the Soko factory which manufactured those helicopters. During the war in Mostar between the Croats and the Bosniaks, Heliodrom was used primarily as a location for arrested Bosniaks, civilians, as well as for the accommodation of various HVO units. And it was also the main logistics centre for food -- for food storage in enormous refrigerators, also a facility to cook that food and for its distribution to the front, and so on. Today --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: -- it is an HVO military base. The 2nd Guards Brigade is situated there, the 2nd Guards Brigade of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Who received you in Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: We were directed by certain groups of soldiers at the Heliodrom towards a small building which had a somewhat larger office on the ground floor. Each person had to give their particulars in that office, their name, surname, their address, and some other information. And after that, the person would be directed to one of the numerous buildings at the Heliodrom which were used for the accommodation of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: To which cell or area, building, you were taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: After our information was taken, I was taken to one of the exercise holes, because earlier, there was a secondary school at the Heliodrom which was used to train pilots. They had two interconnected gyms, sports facilities, and I was taken to one of those holes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: How many prisoners were held along with you in the same room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: When I came, and taking into account both of those holes, which were connected by a corridor, in both of those holes, there was a total of, perhaps, about 500 people. But by the evening, both holes were completely full so that there was a total of 12- to 13-hundred people there. That was the maximum number of people that could fit there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I mean in your room where you were kept.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: The room where I was kept was a smaller room, and there were about 600 people there. We were all lying on the floor. We had one blanket each, some kind of cover, and we were lying on the floor, on the parquet. We were lined -- we were lying down next to each other like sardines in a can. It was very, very tight.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Which administrative or military body was in charge of Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: It's hard to answer that question precisely because in the beginning, the people who were in a very bad -- who were in very bad health would receive certificates of dismissal or of release after undergoing a medical check. They were released home. Those certificates stated, precisely speaking, the Central Military Prison, Heliodrom. And they would be signed by the commander or the administrator, Zvonimir Vidovic. But before the end, this is something that changed many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And who were guards in Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: The guards at the Heliodrom were exclusively military police officers, military police officers of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Could you differentiate them somehow from HVO soldiers from regular troops --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President. But on the last answer, this witness has testified as to who the commander or administrator of the Heliodrom was when he was taken there, and this is an individual that is not showing up on the screen. And for the record, I think it is important that we have the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: There is some problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We could go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Could you repeat the name of the commander in the beginning of your stay in Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Of course, of course I can. The gentleman's name is - and I'll do it letter by letter - was Z-V-O-N-K -- sorry, N-I-M-I-R. There has been a mistake on the screen. "Zvonimir," Z-V-O-N-I-M-I-R, "Zvonimir" V-I-D-O-V-I-C.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Now we should return to my next question. That's about military police and soldiers of HVO regular units.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes. There was a difference between them, because the military police officers had broad white belts around their waists and they also wore other -- the other belts that they wore were white, so you could tell them apart from a great distance and you could differentiate between them and the regular soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you. And just to return to your prison mates, could you tell the Court, of what age were prisoners who were kept in Heliodrom, the range of the ages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: The youngest prisoner in my room was 13 years old. The oldest was about 72 years old. However, afterwards I met even older people, because in the room which was near the room where we went to eat our lunch, I met an old man who was all of 90 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And what about female prisoners, if there were any in Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: In the halls where I was for a few days, there was one single woman. Also, there were no women at the school where I was transferred after four or five days. The first female prisoners that I saw were at the central prison. In the attic of the place where I was kept, that whole area, the attic, was for female prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: What about the conditions of life of prisoners in Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: The living conditions were very bad, practically unbearable. First, the accommodation, the room where I was held, it said on the door that it was 60 square metres, the size -- that the size was 60 square metres. In that space, there was an average of 60 to 80 prisoners. Sometimes there were even 120. So that means that it was half a square metre per prisoner. The food was as follows: In the morning, there would be a cup of tea without sugar and one slice of bread. And then around 7.00 in the evening, the main meal, one tin of fish divided amongst four prisoners or a few spoons of some cooked mixture which, frankly speaking, looked like anything but food. The only thing that there was enough of was water.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: What about medical assistance in Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: A doctor came once a week who was himself a prisoner. Usually, that would be in the evening. Before that, you would have to report to the person on duty, the military police officer on duty, that you wanted to go to see the doctor and why you wanted to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did any representatives of HVO authorities ever visit Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Some representatives of the HVO authorities did come.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: For example, whom do you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: I remember very well that seven or eight days after I came to the camp, when I was already transferred to the school, in the afternoon we were visited by the minister of the Republic of Croatia, Dr. Slobodan Lang, and the chief of the sanitation services of the HV, Dr. Ivan Bagaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did they promise to improve the situation in which the prisoners were held?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: But was that promise ever kept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: No. Unfortunately, the situation was getting worse each day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you ever see representatives of international humanitarian organisations in Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps after about four or five months, sometime in the late autumn, they began to visit from the International Red Cross to register the prisoners and also to bring some essential items like shampoos or -- shampoos against parasites or lice which, due to the bad hygienic conditions, had begun to spread among the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: What do you think; were those visits sort of surprise visits or were they announced before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: No, there were no sudden, unannounced visits allowed. These were visits which were announced in advance each time. At least that is what they told us. And to our questions, why they appeared so late, they told us that their conversations with the HVO about visits were not -- were proceeding with difficulty, and it was only their persistence that allowed them to come and visit us even at such a late stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Were representatives of international organisations allowed to any facilities of the Heliodrom complex, I mean, designed for prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: No, they were not permitted at all to go and visit the rooms in the basement where the prisoners were held and who were completely isolated from other prisoners. There was a large number of foreigners among those prisoners. I remember one American, two Frenchmen, two Germans and some others.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: What about parts of the Heliodrom where female prisoners were held; were they allowed there or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: I think that after a while, after the visit to, let's say, the male section, the International Red Cross went also to visit the female prisoners. But I think that the female prisoners were very strictly guarded to prevent visits to them by foreign TV stations, who had often visited the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness U, did you see any military units deployed in Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, there were numerous HVO units deployed at the Heliodrom, because this is an enormous space, the size practically of a small town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you remember any specific units deployed in Heliodrom? I mean HVO units.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: I saw many members. Very often, I saw members of a unit called "Bruno Busic," members of the Croatian army, and members of the military police, which certainly had a larger unit there in order to secure the entire complex. But certain HVO units had their logistics centres there where they kept food, repaired their weaponry, their motor vehicles, and so on. So that when I looked out of the window from the building where I was being kept, I saw soldiers from all of those units, but I don't know which other units were also deployed there. I think that one anti-terrorist group, I think it was called the ATG Baja Kraljevic, from Siroki Brijeg was there, at least if not permanently, then I think it was there at least for a while deployed at the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you know Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes. Its commander was Predrag Mandic, called "Lija." He was a citizen of Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Will you spell the full name of the commander because, again, it's not in the record.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Of course. Of course. P-R-E-D-R-A-G M-A-N-D-I-C.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And his nickname?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: L-I-J-A. Fox. L-i-j-a, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Sorry. You just mentioned that you saw some members of the Croatian army in Heliodrom. Could you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: From which unit of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: From the 1st Guards Brigade of the regular army of the Republic of Croatia, which was called Tigrovi, "Tigers." And from the 2nd Guards Brigade of the regular Croatian army, which were nicknamed Gromovi, "Thunders." And earlier, there was a unit the size of a brigade from Osijek, the name of which I do not know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Just returning again to the record, this line 17, the first letter "M" in the full name Predrag Mandic is missing, Mandic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, Predrag. Mandic, not Mandac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: It must not be a double D. After D-R in his first name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, there's a mistake. P-R-E-D-R-A-G.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And what kind of functions did those HV units fulfil while staying in the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: This unit from Osijek arrived in mid-July while I was detained at school. With its available artillery, it tried to sever the communications between the city of Mostar, the centre, and the Blagaj settlement, which is 10 kilometres to the south. That was probably their objective, to cut those communications in order to cut off the southern area, the southern part from the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you know if these or other HV units were involved in military operations in the territory of Mostar or close to Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Of course. Of course. This unit was on combat activity all day in the direction of Mostar, the southern exit of Mostar. And it had considerable support from artillery weapons; however, for some reason, things turned badly for them. And we found out later that they suffered large losses. They withdrew from their positions and disappeared in an unknown direction. I think they had 50 of their soldiers killed that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you have any personal conversations with the members of the Croat army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: I spent two full months as a prisoner, as a captive, working in a unit of the Croatian army which was stationed at the Heliodrom, but I worked in a unit which was a mixed mortar battery. I worked continually for two months in that unit every day from 8.00 in the morning to 7.00 at night, every day. I cleaned the officers' and the soldiers' rooms, cleaned the bathrooms, cooked some food for them. Mostly, I made coffee, and I talked a lot with them. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: You worked inside the Heliodrom complex?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: No. This was about 6 kilometres outside of the Heliodrom complex. We went out in their trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Just to clarify, to which unit did these soldiers belong? I mean the soldiers for whom you were performing some job.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: I think this was the 3rd battalion of the 2nd brigade of the regular army of the Republic of Croatia, Gromovi. The command was located at the Heliodrom, and they would take us every morning to work, 6 kilometres away from Heliodrom, to their positions where these mortar batteries were located. And they would bring us back at 7.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you remember if other prisoners were also taken outside of Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: A very large number. The smallest number of prisoners worked at the Heliodrom itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: For what purposes were they taken outside of Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: The most frequent reason for this, for taking them away from the Heliodrom, was to go to the front line of the HVO Defence where they mainly repaired or built new bunkers, fortifications of the lines, and other jobs. But 90 percent of these jobs were actually done on those facilities. The remaining -- the other cases of taking people away from the Heliodrom was to take people to paint someone else's houses, to repair it, to cut wood and other business. Every prisoner, in other words, had a job to perform.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: You were involved in this kind of forced labour on the confrontation line? I mean you, personally.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: I wasn't. Me and my older brother, there were nine members of my family at the Heliodrom. For some reason or other, we were forbidden to go out, to work outside the premises of the Heliodrom. It was only when the Croatian army came, then this provision was no longer valid. It was only two months during my entire stay at the Heliodrom that I worked for the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And how did this procedure of taking prisoners for forced labour work in Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: There was no particular time. Each time when the heavy metal door was heard leading to our -- the place where we were accommodated, all the prisoners from all three large rooms had to go to the corridor and line up, looking at the floor. The military police or the representatives of some of the units who required some prisoners chose a certain number of prisoners, the prisoners that they wished. And this happened during the entire 24 hours of the day, round the clock, and very frequently even after midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you remember any people that were familiar to you and who were taking prisoners for forced labour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Of course I remember. I remember many prisoners. Out of the 60 -- all of the 60 or 70 people in my room had to go to forced labour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Witness. You haven't understood me rightly. I'm asking about people who were taking prisoners for forced labour. You mentioned that there were military police representatives and some other people who entered Heliodrom and used to take prisoners for forced labour. I asked: Who were those people who were taking prisoners, if you remember any of the names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Of course the members of practically all the HVO units would come for the prisoners. The misunderstanding was the members of the military police only took them out of the building and handed them over to the people who required prisoners. For instance, the Vinko Skrobo unit, the Benko Penavic unit, and all the other HVO units would take prisoners, so that sometimes at some moments during the day, even more than 80 per cent of the prisoners had to perform forced labour. And of course I remember the names of the persons that would come. Sometimes they simply entered the rooms and chose -- and usually chose the stronger persons because they had to do heavy-duty labour. I can perhaps mention some of the names of these persons that would come.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Please, if you can, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Of course. From the 1st Battalion of the 2nd HVO Brigade, from the Bojna prison, there was a young man by the name of Drazen Sunjic who would come frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Please spell his first name and full name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes. D-R-A-Z-E-N, S-U-N-J-I-C. And the other young man that would take the -- to take these people to the unit, probably from the Benko Penavic or Vinko Skrobo units, (redacted) (redacted). His name was Miro Primorac. In other words, M-I-R-O, P-R-I-M-O-R-A-C [realtime transcript read in error "P-R-A-I-M-O-R-A-C"]. I saw on a number of occasions one of the people who -- that was very close to Mr. Martinovic, whose name was "Dubravko Pehar."

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Please spell it again.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: D-U-B-R-A-V-K-O, P-E-H-A-R [realtime transcript read in error "D-E-H-A-R"]. There's something wrong here. I shall repeat. P-E-H-A-R.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: So it is pronounced "Pehar"; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: "Pehar", that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: If we can return to -- you gave one name like "Primorac," if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: We have a spelling mistake here on line 43. We have here "Praimorac."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: "Primorac" is the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: So the "A" before the "I" should be removed. Do you remember, Witness U, if there were any wounded or killed among prisoners who were taken to perform forced labour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
