utterances.text: Of course. There was a large number of wounded, especially in periods -- in some periods. I remember the night of 30th to 31st of August, 1993, when in my room alone 20 wounded persons were brought. And according to the stories of the other prisoners, on that particular night there were 10 or 11 persons killed and over 150 wounded, only on that night, on that night alone, this -- one of the attempts of the HVO to go through the separation line in the city, to penetrate that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness U, another question that is about the manner in which prisoners were treated by the guards and other people who had access to Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: The treatment by the guards was, generally speaking, bad. Quite sincerely, this depended from one man to another. There were people who availed themselves of every opportunity to do ill to the prisoners, to provoke them, to humiliate them, to offend them. There were also good guys who comforted us, told us that it would all end, and who offered us cigarettes and bread, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you remember if any other military people from HVO had access to Heliodrom, I mean apart from military police who were officially guarding you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: I believe that all the soldiers of the HVO, especially the commanders, had every possibility to enter the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember a prisoner whose name was "Haramandzic"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the name?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: "Haramandzic" [realtime transcript read in error "Her Mandzic"].

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes. I thought that you had said "Mandzic." Haramandzic, yes, I remember him very well. We were acquaintances for many years and friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes. I see again here in the minutes we have "Her Mandzic."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: His name was H-A-R-A-M-A-N-D-Z-I-C, "Haramandzic."

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: This will not be a very long question, but I would ask Your Honour to go into private session because our witness may give a name of a person who may be called as a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: So what happened then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.01 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President and Your Honours, I just want to take a moment of your time and ask you if, immediately prior to recess today at 4.00, if I could have one minute of your time before you leave on an issue concerning the physical health of my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you mean you'll talk to me in the court?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, in the court. All three of Your Honours, before you go to chambers this afternoon, in open court I would just like a moment of your time before you recess today. In open court, Your Honour, yes. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. Mr. Prosecutor, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness U, when were you released from Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: There are two dates. I was released on the 15th of December, 1993, through a humanitarian German agency which released people of mixed marriages. And since my wife is a Serb, I was in the selection of those who were released from the Heliodrom, and we received assurances that we could go to a third country. However, since my family was on the left bank, I applied to go to the left bank, but the bus brought us to the western part of town and they simply left us there on the street. Luckily, there were offices of the International Red Cross nearby, so we asked them either to return us to where we came -- either to take us to where we were supposed to go or to take us back to the prison, which they managed to do. So in fact we were returned to the prison at Heliodrom. And then on the 18th, again I was released, and I arrived on the left bank in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to go into private session for some minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Is there any particular reason for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, because now we'll talk about our witness postwar, following the war, his occupation, and it may reveal his identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll go into the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we are in the open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness U, somewhere in the middle of your testimony, you mentioned that you had known Stela or Vinko Martinovic before the war. Could you expand a little bit on this issue, if you really knew him pretty well and his family as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you know about some criminal proceedings against Stela when he was a young man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Well, I knew as much as his friends knew, the company he kept. I knew that he had some problems because of minor misdemeanours and that he ended up at the correctional facility in Stolac. But I'm not really expert in that area, so I don't know whether he was tried or not. But I know that Mr. Martinovic, in his early youth, was quite a lively young man and, unfortunately, he was prone to minor criminal acts, and that is why he ended up in a juvenile correctional facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I have completed my examination-in-chief. In the end, I would ask you -- I would like to tender into evidence Exhibit Number 11.18 under the seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we'll come to this stage later. I think the number should be another number, because this evidence is marked by the witness himself.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The correct number is P11.18/2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any cross-examination? Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Let me introduce myself. I am Kresimir Krsnik, and I am the Defence counsel of the accused Mladen Naletilic. I will be asking you questions. As I warn every witness, I try to pose very concise questions in order to receive a very concise answer, so please do not go into any interpretations but respond as precisely as possible to my questions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I think that we should go into --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I agree. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Okay. Private session.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

If you allow me, I would like to ask the witness whether he recalls this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember it. I don't see my signature there, and this is not a usual way of greetings in the document.

utterances.text: No, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: On the left, it says: "Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, B and H Army, Military Unit, Defence of the Republic." It says --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Please read it as it is written. It says "Obrana," not "Odbrana."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: "Defence of the Republic, Military Secret, Classified. Proposal for the cover of the intelligence service of Mostar." "Second Department," you said you didn't know what the second department was. I will now read, and perhaps that will remind you. "The chief and the operatives of the Intelligence Operative Centre, Mostar, thought about some kind of activity in order to conceal or cover the work and the activity of this centre. In view of the fact that Mostar is a very specific environment and a town which has undergone double aggression, i.e., aggression first by the SCA and then a bloody one-year aggression by the HVO and the HV, and also having in mind that both the aggressors are still quite close to the town, and that also in the city itself, on various pretexts, there are thousands of foreigners, i.e., that there are already many intelligence services of European countries in the town itself, believe that the cover for the work of the intelligence department centre in Mostar could most favourably be provided by the forming of an agency for the search of missing persons during combat operations. This agency would be of a humanitarian character, i.e., it would be searching for all missing persons from this area without charging for its services, and it would be financed by contributions and donations. There is a need for this, because the vast number of people from this area, there is no information other than that they have been displaced throughout the world. Many of them have probably been killed, and a large number is currently in Chetnik jails and jails of the HVO. We would try not only to make this agency official, but we would also include it in the network of similar humanitarian agencies throughout Europe, which would provide the ideal possibility to the operatives and those working with the agency, cooperating with it, i.e., the intelligence department of the Mostar centre."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: I apologise, but I am receiving a French translation in my headphones. I just wanted to let you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I think we stopped at the place: "... the intelligence department of the Mostar centre, to travel to all regions of interest to us. This would enable them, using the ID of the agency, which we would try to obtain international verification for, so this would provide them access to all places of interest for strong reasons, i.e., the search of missing or allegedly missing persons. For a start, we would gather a large amount of data about missing persons, which is not difficult because this data already exists in certain literature. And after processing this information, we would make a plan to tour all the places of interest, of course from the military intelligence aspect. Such work would provide the opportunity also to develop a network of cooperation in the area of former Yugoslavia and broader. Kindly respond to this brief proposal, and if necessary we can elaborate the proposal with many more details. "Best regards, M. S." I would now request that we go into the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll go into private session. Mr. Krsnik, that's quite a long paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Sorry. [Interpretation] Your Honour, had I had the time, we would have obtained a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: May it please the Trial Chamber, if the witness is finished for today, I would wait until he leaves before I make my statements to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. The usher may take the witness out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: May it please the Trial Chamber, Your Honours, thank you very much. It has come to my attention today, and we have brought this matter to the attention of the Trial Chamber almost two weeks ago, and that is my client is suffering from a very bad infection on his tooth. This infection now has gone up to his sinuses. Almost two weeks ago, Your Honour, Mr. President, indicated, after speaking with the registrar, that he would have an appointment with a dentist. We just found out today he has no appointment, has not had an appointment with the dentist. But the registrar tells us that Thursday morning at 11.00 a.m., he will have an appointment with the dentist. We want to -- and we're not saying that it's anybody's fault, but we cannot understand why this problem cannot be taken care of. He has been on antibiotics. However, because of his heart problem, the infection in his tooth, if it spreads - which we believe it has spread to his sinus area - if it spreads to his heart, he could die. We do not want to stop Mr. Naletilic from having his dentist appointment on Thursday at 11.00 a.m. We want to make sure that he has that appointment. However, we do not waive the right for Mr. Naletilic to be absent from these proceedings. We want him and he wants to be here, and he needs to be here for these proceedings. So we request that on Thursday, that we take some breaks to allow Mr. Naletilic to go to the dentist's office, have his work done, and then returned to the courtroom and resume the proceedings at that time. We respectfully request that. We believe that Mr. Naletilic has every absolute fundamental right to be present at all critical junctures in the proceedings, and the trial is a critical juncture, obviously, in this proceeding, and we do not believe that he should be absent. So we're only merely requesting that on this Thursday, this Honourable Trial Chamber recesses while this work is completed. Otherwise, we are afraid that they will bring him to court Thursday morning and then he will not see the dentist again, and it will be another two weeks and matters will deteriorate further. That's my concern, Your Honours. I would also like to say that Mr. Naletilic has expressed to us specifically today, more so than yesterday but today especially, he's in much pain. He has been taken off any pain medication. For some reason, they are not giving him any pain medication, and he needs his pain medication. Without his pain medication, it is very hard for him to follow these proceedings, to assist counsel in listening to and collating the information coming from the witness stand so as to be able to alert Defence counsel to any possible questions that might be asked in cross-examination. We do not know why he is not receiving his pain medication until the date that he can see the dentist and have this problem taken care of. We do not -- I don't want to belabour this any longer, but these are very serious matters, Your Honour, especially with the heart condition with which Mr. Naletilic suffers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Meek, for bringing this matter to our attention. As a matter of fact, this Trial Chamber has looked into this matter and instructed the registrar to make dentist appointments for your client. And I saw Mr. Scott standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I feel I have to respond to a couple of points. First of all, the Prosecution has never been anything less than supportive of any bona fide health concerns raised by the Defence, and that continues to be the case. Having said that, Your Honours, we are concerned. The witnesses who come here also have certain rights and, I think, should be treated fairly. And we have witnesses who are here, and some of them have now Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. come here and stayed for a long time. We have scheduled four additional witnesses for the balance of this week. As the Chamber knows, we're not in session next week. That means that if we do not finish these witnesses by the end of this week, we have the situation of sending these witnesses back, and they may or may not come back in the future. Now, in terms of the cross-examination, far be it from me to tell Mr. Krsnik how to conduct his cross-examination. However, if he wants to allocate 25 minutes of his time talking about Muslim versus Bosniak religion and all those sorts of things, I submit to you that should not be done at the expense of the witnesses who come to The Hague to testify, and that has to be allocated against his reasonable amount of cross-examination time. Further, further, if there is going to be a break in the trial schedule on Thursday because of these health issues, then we would have no choice - and my apologies to the Chamber if it causes any inconvenience - we would have no choice but to then seek to make up that time by going into court -- by holding court on Thursday evening and as late on Friday as necessary to complete these four witnesses so they can return to Bosnia without being required to come back again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: May it please the Trial Chamber. And no disrespect to my learned friend on the other side, my question was about the tooth problem of my client. Now, in the country which I come from, and I think that in this country also, my client can see a dentist in the evening. My client can see a dentist at 5.00 or 5.30. He doesn't have to see a dentist in the middle of the day. And I also, Your Honour, believe that it's inappropriate for Mr. Scott to comment on Mr. Krsnik's cross-examination, especially when his cross-examination is about a relevant point, and that is language. You understand, everybody here understands, that the Prosecution has made allegations in this indictment alleging certain things about the language of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Croatian language, and we have to address those in cross-examination. I understand that this last witness has been a problematic witness. Now, the problems stemming from this witness may be two-fold, three-fold, or more. But from where I sit, I see a witness who doesn't wait for a question to be finished but starts the answer. So I don't believe it's a one-way street, and I believe that the Trial Chamber also sees it that way. If Mr. Scott believes that this is not a bona fide problem, please let him tell the Trial Chamber why he thinks that my client's tooth problem and infection and heart problem is not serious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. I just want to say two sentences. Your Honours, my learned friend Scott has touched upon a very important point regarding cross-examination. If my learned friend Krsnik did not ask questions which pertain to facts, and the context in which Croatia invaded Bosnia and Herzegovina, imposed its language, imposed its currency, and also imposed its culture by destroying monuments, if my colleague Krsnik did not pose such questions, I, myself, or my colleague Par would ask these questions. So if Mr. Krsnik covers these questions -- if he didn't cover these questions, we would cover them. If the Prosecution has a problem with that, then they can just delete it from the indictment, and then our job would be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, after hearing the views from both sides, especially after the request from Mr. Meek concerning your client's healthiness, this Trial Chamber will make its decision concerning the further proceedings, especially on Thursday, at a later stage. Maybe tomorrow morning. We have to adjourn at this moment. Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I want to thank you very much, Mr. President and Your Honours. I only have one other question, and maybe it's to the registrar. Mr. Scott was nice enough to deliver to me an order and search warrant on the Tobacco Station in Siroki Brijeg dated -- issued 18th of September, 1998. However, Mr. Scott indicated he believed that the information which was delivered to Judge May in order for him to find probable cause to sign this document, this search warrant, it may be under seal. I'm just asking for directions from either the registrar or from the Trial Chamber as to where I might be able to obtain those documents so that I can adequately prepare arguments to this Trial Chamber as to why these documents should not be admitted; or, if I read those documents, perhaps I won't make that argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We have to make an inquiry before we give you a proper answer. So we are adjourned until 9.30 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: 4.05 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 26th day of September, 2001, at 9.30 a.m.
